Bādarāyaṇa
------------------------------------------
Vedānta is the last of the six systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्. बादरायण is stated to be its author. Hindu tradition identifies him with Veda-व्यास (also known as Kṛṣna द्वैपायन), the celebrated author of the Mahābhārata. Lexicographers like Hemacandra (A.

-1173) (vide his Abhidhānacintāmaṇi—Martyakāṇḍa, 512) support this view. Since he lived along with his disciples and son शुक, at the Badarī in the हिमालयस्, he might have used this name in his composition, the Brahmasūtras.
Bādarāyaṇa appears in the Sāma-vidhāna Brāhmaṇa of the Sāmaveda. वराहमिहिर (A.

-587) and Bhaṭṭotpala (10th cent. A. D.) well-known astronomers, have mentioned another बादरायण in their works. But, they are different from बादरायण-व्यास.
See also VYĀSA.

Badarīnātha
(‘Lord of Badarī’)
------------------------------------------
Tīrthayātrā or पिल्ग्रिमगे to holy places has been an age-old exercise under-taken by the pious Hindus. The हिमालयस् and the river गङ्गा have so captivated the Hindu मिन्द् for generations that a majority of these places of पिल्ग्रिमगे is associated with them. बदरीनाथ, also spelt as Badrināth, situated in the Chamoli district of Uttaranchal, is one of the most important of these and has been classed among the ‘Caturdhāmas’ (the four Holy Places), the other three being द्वारका in Western India, पुरी in Eastern India and रामेश्वरम् in South India. A visit to these four places has been a life-time’s ambition of many a devout Hindu since it is as good as covering all important places of पिल्ग्रिमगे in the country.
The place itself might have derived its name from the existence of Badarī or the jujube tree in plenty in that area.
Even from the most ancient days, बदरीनाथ has been considered as very sacred. It was known as बदरिकाश्रम. It was here that the twin sages, नर-नारायण, had built their hermitage and performed severe austerities. The sage पराशर and व्यास, the celebrated author of the महाभारत, lived here with their disciples. Consequently व्यास got the by-name बादरायण.
The town is situated at a height of about 7000 metres (23,300 ft.), in a valley nearly 6 kms. long and 2 kms. wide (4 miles by 1.3 miles). The temple is on the right bank of the river अलकनन्दा.
The original temple is said to have been built by Śaṅkarācārya in the 8th century A.D., after recovering the old image from the नारद Kuṇḍa (pond). Over the centuries, avalanches washed out many a temple and the present one is comparatively a modern structure.
Near the temple is a hot-water pond called ‘Taptakuṇḍa’, with a thermal spring of sulphurous waters. A bath here is a must, before the visit to the temple.
The temple of Lord नारायण is about 13.5 metres (45 ft.) in height and faces east. There is a golden कलश or pinnacle on the top. The image inside the temple is made of ‘śālagrāmaśilā’ or black stone. It is in the पद्मासन or seated posture, with four arms, carrying the well-known symbols शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus), गदा (mace) and पद्म (lotus). Other images found in the temple are those of नर and नारायण, उद्धव, नारद, गरुड and कुबेर.
The chief priest called ‘Rāval’ is a नम्बूदिरि ब्राह्मण from Kerala, as per the traditions established by Śaṅkarācārya.
The temple, being situated among the mountains of the Himālayan snow range, is open to the devotees only for about six months (April-May to November). The उत्सवमूर्ति (image used in temple processions) is shifted to the temple of नरसिṁह at Joshimath, a place situated at a distance of 48 kms (31 miles) from Badarinath and worshipped there during the winter months. The chief priest and his entourage also shift to this place for this purpose. The ‘Jyotirmaṭha,’ one of the four principal monasteries established by Śaṅkarācārya is also situated here.
Lord बदरीनाथ is worshipped in five different places. Hence they are collectively called ‘Pañcabadarīs.’ They are: Viśāla Badarī (the main Badarīnath); Yogadhyāna Badarī (at Pāṇḍukeśvara, about 24 kms. [16 miles] away from Badarīnath); Bhaviṣya Badarī (near Tapovana, about 17 kms. [11 miles] away from the Joshimath); Vṛddha Badarī (at Animath, 17 kms. from Joshimath in the direction of Pipalkot) and Ādi Badarī (about 16 kms. [10 miles] from कर्ण-prayāg on the road to Rāṇikhet).
It is believed that if śrāddha (obsequial ceremonies) is offered here at the place called ‘Brahmakapāla’ on the bank of अलकनन्दा to the dead ancestors, they are liberated at once. Hence it is no more necessary to continue the annual śrāddhas.

Bādāmi
------------------------------------------
Nestling at the foot of steep hills, this small town is situated in the Bijapur district of Karnataka State. Known as वातापि in the ancient days, it was the capital of the Cālukyan empire during the period A.

-753. It contains several temples of the structural as well as the rock-cut varieties. Near the fort there are temples dedicated to हनुमान् and शिव. On the southern hill, situated on its western side, there are four cave-temples (three Hindu and one Jain). They resemble the ones at एल्लोर. The pillared halls in them show a high standard of workmanship and are uniformly of the same appearance. The pillars are mostly square in section though a few of the inner colonnade in Cave no.3 are multifaceted.
बादामि">Mālegitti Śivālaya at BādāmiIn the first cave are seen images of शिव with 18 arms, गणेश, विष्णु, लक्ष्मी as also शिव-पार्वती. The back wall contains panel-figures of Mahiṣāsuramardinī (Durgā), गणेश and स्कन्द. The second cave contains images of वामन, Varāha, नारायण on गरुड and नारायण on the serpent शेष. The third cave has images and figures of Ardhanārīśvara, पार्वती, नरसिṁह and Varāha. The fourth cave contains the images of the Jain Tīrthaṅkaras.
Among the structural temples, the Mālegitti Śivālaya built on a hill over-looking the town of बादामि needs special mention. It is a massive solid structure, though not very large. It consists of a cella, an assembly hall and a porch.
There are fine frescos, very much like those of Ajanta, in Cave no. 3. The most important and well-preserved of these is that of the betrothal of पार्वती to शिव. These paintings belong to the 6th century A. D.
See also AIHOḶE and PATTADAKAL.
